## The problem

Full-text search matches words exactly as they were indexed. SQLite’s
FTS5, the full-text engine litesearch uses, splits text into tokens with
a tokenizer and stores every token in an index; a query matches a row
only when the query’s tokens are in that index. Sanskrit breaks this in
three ways. The same word can be printed in Devanagari or in IAST, the
Latin transliteration with diacritics. Vedic texts add tone marks above
and below the letters. And many readers type a plain-English spelling
with no diacritics at all. Before this module, these searches found
nothing:

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>query</th>
<th>against</th>
<th>hits</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>देवी</code></td>
<td><code>दे॒वी</code>, the same word with Vedic accents</td>
<td>0</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>श्रीमाता</code></td>
<td><code>śrīmātā</code>, the same word in IAST</td>
<td>0</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>kuṇḍa</code></td>
<td><code>cidagnikuṇḍasambhūtā</code></td>
<td>0</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

The fix is to reduce every word, whatever its script, to a lossy ASCII
key when it is indexed, and to do the same to the query. `श्रीमाता`,
`śrīmātā` and `srimata` all become `srimata`, so each of them finds the
other two. Nothing is transliterated at query time and no second column
is added.

Every store litesearch creates uses this, Sanskrit or not. English text
keeps its own tokens, so an English search behaves as before, but the
extra keys do take space: on this repository’s notebooks the FTS index
grows 14.7%. Metre, verse chunking, citations beyond the pattern below,
and lemmas live in [ganapati](https://github.com/vedicreader/ganapati).

## Folding a word

Folding means mapping several spellings of a word to one key. This
module folds at two strengths.

[`fold_token`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/sanskrit.html#fold_token)
is the strict fold. It removes Vedic tone marks
([`strip_vedic`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/sanskrit.html#strip_vedic)),
turns Devanagari into ASCII letter by letter
([`deva2ascii`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/sanskrit.html#deva2ascii)),
and strips diacritics from Latin letters. Aspirates survive: `भीष्म`
folds to `bhisma` and `kṛṣṇa` to `krsna`, and the consonants ś, ṣ and s
all become `s`.
[`detect_script`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/sanskrit.html#detect_script)
reports whether a string is mostly Devanagari or Latin.

[`roman_fold`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/sanskrit.html#roman_fold)
is the loose fold, built on
[`fold_token`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/sanskrit.html#fold_token)
for readers who type English spellings. It drops the `h` after a
consonant (so bh, ch, dh, kh, sh, th all lose it), shortens ee to i, oo
to u and any doubled vowel to one, turns w into v, and reads `ri` before
a consonant as the vowel ṛ. `Bheeshma`, `Bhishma`, `Bhīṣma` and `भीष्म`
all become `bisma`; `Krishna` and `कृष्ण` become `krsna`; `chandra` and
`चन्द्र` become `candra`. The `ri` rule also catches words that never had
a ṛ, so `śrīmātā` folds to `srmata`. That is harmless in an index,
because the query folds the same way.

[`skeleton`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/sanskrit.html#skeleton)
goes further still and keeps a folded word’s first letter and its
consonants, with vowels and `y` removed and repeated letters collapsed:
`saundarya` and `soundarya` both become `sndr`. It is too loose for an
index. `correct(skeleton=True)` uses it as a last resort when looking
for the index term a misspelled query word was meant to be.

``` python
assert roman_fold('02', numbers=True) == '2' and roman_fold('02') == '02'
assert skeleton(roman_fold('saundarya')) == skeleton(roman_fold('soundarya'))
assert skeleton('laharii') == 'lhr' and skeleton('sukra') != skeleton('sukta')
```

Reading the tests above as examples: `roman_fold('Bheeshma')` is
`bisma`, the same key as `भीष्म`, `Bhīṣma` and `Bhishma`. Distinct names
stay distinct, so `agni` and `aṅga` do not meet.

The FTS5 tokenizer below emits the
[`roman_fold`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/sanskrit.html#roman_fold)
key as one more token beside each word whose strict fold is at least
four letters long. That third token is what lets `Bheeshma` reach `भीष्म`
and `Bhīṣma` in a search. On this repository’s notebooks it grows the
FTS index by 14.7%, from 178,705 to 204,979 bytes.

[`roman_fold`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/sanskrit.html#roman_fold)
has three switches, all off by default and all off in the tokenizer.
They are for matching a reader’s word against a list of known words, not
for building an index. `doubles=True` collapses a doubled letter, so
`Raghuvamsha` and `Raghuvaṃśa` meet. `endings=True` cuts an English
plural or past ending when three letters remain, so `duties` and `duty`
both become `dut`. `numbers=True` reads a string of digits as a number,
so `02` becomes `2`.

``` python
from fastcore.test import test_eq
test_eq(roman_fold('Lakshmana'), 'laksmana'); test_eq(roman_fold('Lakshmana'), roman_fold('Lakṣmaṇa'))
test_eq(roman_fold('Lakkshmana', doubles=True), roman_fold('Lakṣmaṇa'))
test_eq(roman_fold('Raghuvamsha', doubles=True), roman_fold('Raghuvaṃśa', doubles=True))
test_eq(roman_fold('duties', endings=True), roman_fold('duty', endings=True))
test_eq(roman_fold('worshipped', doubles=True, endings=True), 'vorsip')
test_eq(roman_fold('yes', endings=True), 'yes')   # three letters stay
test_eq(roman_fold('duties'), 'duties')            # both off by default
test_eq(roman_fold('11', doubles=True, numbers=True), '11')   # a digit is no letter: 11 stays eleven
test_eq(roman_fold('0100', doubles=True, numbers=True), '100')
test_eq(roman_fold('திருக்குறள்', doubles=True), roman_fold('திருக்குறள்'))   # a script fold_token leaves as it is keeps its letters
```

## The tokenizer

An FTS5 tokenizer is the function that turns a row’s text into the
tokens the index stores, and a query’s text into the tokens it looks up.
FTS5 lets tokenizers wrap each other: in a chain such as
`porter unicode61`, `unicode61` splits the text into words and `porter`
stems each word it receives, so `running` is stored as `run`.

[`sanskrit_tokenizer`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/sanskrit.html#sanskrit_tokenizer)
is a wrapping tokenizer of that kind. It asks the tokenizer inside it
for words and passes each word on together with its
[`fold_token`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/sanskrit.html#fold_token)
key and, for longer words, its
[`roman_fold`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/sanskrit.html#roman_fold)
key. FTS5 calls tokens that share a position colocated: they count as
the same word, so a query matches the row through any of them. The
original word is kept, so nothing an English search relied on is lost.
Passing `original=0` drops it and keeps only the keys.

`SANSKRIT_TOKENIZE` is the tokenizer’s registered name, `'sanskrit'`.
litesearch’s default chain, `_FTS_TOKENIZE` in `litesearch.core`, is
`porter simplify casefold 1 sanskrit unicodewords`. Read it from the
right: apsw’s `unicodewords` splits words by the Unicode rules and keeps
`fts_search` whole, `sanskrit` adds the folded keys,
`simplify casefold 1` lowercases every token without removing
diacritics, and `porter` stems English. `sanskrit` has to sit inside
`porter`. If it wrapped porter instead, it would fold porter’s output,
the index would hold `dharmaksetre` while the query `dharmaksetre` stems
to `dharmaksetr`, and the search would miss. The regression test below
checks exactly this case.

A store’s tokenizer is fixed when its FTS table is created.
[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database)
registers `sanskrit` on every connection it opens, and
[`register_sanskrit`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/sanskrit.html#register_sanskrit)
does the same for a connection you opened yourself. A connection without
it, such as Python’s `sqlite3` module or the `sqlite3` shell, can still
read the store’s ordinary columns, but every FTS query and every insert
into the store fails with `error in tokenizer constructor`, because the
insert triggers update the FTS index.

## Citations

GRETIL, the Göttingen archive of Sanskrit e-texts, marks each verse with
its address between double bars or double slashes, as in `// Mn_1.1 //`
(Manusmṛti 1.1) or `|| BrhUp_1,1.2 ||`. `CITE_RE` finds these markers
and
[`cite_parts`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/sanskrit.html#cite_parts)
splits one into its siglum, the abbreviation for the work, and its
numbered levels. `litesearch.tree` builds a document’s tree from them,
so a GRETIL text gets chapters and verses as sections with no other
markup.

### cite_parts

``` python
    c:str

```

*Split a citation into its siglum and its levels: `'BrhUp_1,1.2'` gives
`('BrhUp', ['1','1','2'])`.*

``` python
from litesearch.sanskrit import cite_parts

assert cite_parts('BrhUp_1,1.2') == ('BrhUp', ['1','1','2'])
assert cite_parts('Mn_1.1') == ('Mn', ['1','1'])
assert cite_parts('IsUp_4[57M]') == ('IsUp', ['4'])      # the alternate-edition number is dropped
assert cite_parts('not a citation') == ('not a citation', [])
```
